C01.note: High: a signed, one-night grant of named reversible actions makes approval the feature, it acts on real Cloud Run traffic and flags, and the dark phone lands in seconds. Low if the night start through the Flows API fails and the 3am scene becomes a scripted replay.

C02.note: High: the dark phone and a code floor the model can only raise. Low: it changes nothing in production, so on video it reads as alert triage, and Night Orders tells the same bedroom story with real action.

C03.note: High: real experiments on no-traffic Cloud Run revisions hand a half-awake engineer tested options, not guesses. Low: replaying a production failure on staging is fragile, and the hero shot is three small charts rather than a person.

C04.note: High: the alarm comes from people, the agent reproduces before it pages, then closes the gap with a new monitor and a reply to the nurse who asked if it was just her. Low if the Service Desk start or the timed count cannot fire a flow and the tickets look canned.

C05.note: High: it owns the leftovers nobody owns after an incident, with a count that must balance before close. Low: the 3am changes must be staged by script, and flag, silence and scaling history may not be readable with our role.

C06.note: High: alert rule changes proven by backtest against real incidents before anyone approves, applied to Cloud Monitoring as code. Low: needs weeks of seeded metric history and the hero is a chart, which edges toward a dashboard.

C07.note: High: a scared new hire meets the failure first on a Thursday afternoon, and the drill fixes rotten runbook steps. Low: close to the crowded onboarding aids, and a staged fault can look like a toy.

C08.note: High: two clocks, moon and sun, and a helper who says yes before anyone is woken. Low: only two stages, the agent mostly routes a message, and the demo needs two real accounts plus an outside timer.

C09.note: High: a truly hands-off production rollout whose rule is who is awake, in the open configure stage. Low: the model only picks signals and explains, so the agent looks thin next to plain scheduled code, and days of rollout need time compression.

C10.note: High: Ana's flight to her sister's wedding and the closing line 'You were not needed.' Low: the agent mostly interviews in an issue, Google Cloud is barely used, and it sits next to LORE's organizational memory.

C11.note: High: real rehearsal of old code on the new schema plus an expand and contract split. Low: on video it is a release gate next to BABYDOV's rollback rehearsal, and ORM details can eat the build.

C12.note: High: opens on one shop owner, changes who gets the fix first through a real flag user list, and his 'works!' informs a person's decision to widen. Low if it reads as a 'your bug is fixed' email, which judges file with Proof of Fix, or the Service Desk round trip fails.

C13.note: High: the black screen and 'button, button, button' land in seconds, the model really drives a keyboard journey, and the impact is concrete (Cloud Text-to-Speech fits naturally). Low if the browser cannot run in the flow and it shrinks to a scripted accessibility test that gates releases.

C14.note: High: proof by test on old and new lockfiles, real evidence rather than a summary. Low: crowded dependency and security bot space, little Google Cloud, and the demo is a table.

C15.note: High: guards the least touched package stage and only ever keeps, which is safe to run alone. Low: the hero moment is a non-event, the model's share is thin, and it reads as a nightly report.

C16.note: High: the agent builds the off switch, its alert and the runbook line before merge and proves the off state is safe, so 3am is one tap. Low: it starts as a pre-merge code edit near crowded review tools, and an automated refactor can break things.

C17.note: High: the deepest natural Google Cloud use in the pool (Cloud Logging plus Sensitive Data Protection) with a named approver for the cleanup. Low: same mechanism as Proof of Fix, and no person a viewer will remember.

C18.note: High: people's own words, matched to the flag cohort by code, can hold a rollout step. Low: needs believable seeded ticket volume, Google Cloud plays little part, and Front Row tells a warmer version.

C19.note: High: inventive governance that raises the guard and always returns to the baseline people wrote. Low: the payoff is a settings panel changing, it needs Maintainer and Premium features, and it sits near BABYDOV's autonomy budget.

C20.note: High: 'You said you'd revisit' and an MR that keeps a tired engineer's promise. Low: telling a temporary patch from normal work is fuzzy, and writing the proper fix in general is hard to show honestly.

C21.note: High: a funny, clear hook ('give me one reason to live') and real dead code removal in the open configure stage. Low: flag cleanup tools exist, the stakes feel small, and Google Cloud barely appears.

C22.note: High: the most original question in the pool, do our incident rituals work, answered with a control group. Low: needs many past incidents with metrics that must be generated, and the result is an analysis chart, not an action.

C23.note: High: a new give-back loop that pays upstream with a minimal reproduction before upgrading. Low: the upstream fix must be staged with our own library, the story spans weeks, and Google Cloud has no role.

C24.note: High: the line 'it is flaky, it is not you'. Low: beside the excluded CI failure fixers and existing flaky test tools, no Google Cloud, and weeks of staged retries.

C25.note: High only as a trust layer on another product. Low: GitLab's own Review instructions learner and LORE already occupy it, it needs other agents to be corrected first, and nothing happens in production.

C26.note: High: an untouched space, people leaving, where every finding is checked against the API before a successor takes it. Low: the output is a checklist, reading others' schedules and approvals may need Maintainer, and Google Cloud is barely involved.

C27.note: High: deep, natural Google Cloud use (live Cloud Run config, Cloud Audit Logs, keyless auth) and a deploy that refuses to erase a person's 2am fix. Low if the drift check cannot start a flow without a person or the deploy guard needs Maintainer on main.

C28.note: High: makes the human approval itself the feature, one cited question at the moment of consent. Low: a single step that can read as a smarter MR summary, with little to show in Google Cloud.

C29.note: High: autonomy is the product, earned per action through a merge and lost on the first miss, which answers the theme head on. Low: six approvals of history must be staged, and unless the permit MR is the hero it looks like BABYDOV's autonomy budget.

C30.note: High: Kemi's smile and closing the loop to the author. Low: a report at heart, a summary in disguise, and it sits next to Proof of Fix and Stayed Shipped.

C31.note: High: a real compliance pain answered by code from records GitLab already keeps. Low: a question and answer bot over records, next to the crowded evidence receipts space, with no scene to film.

C32.note: High: real traffic in Cloud Logging names the last callers, like a school library, and removal waits in escrow until zero. Low: weeks of traffic must be compressed into a labelled clock with seeded callers, which can feel staged.

C33.note: High: honest, code-checked status for one customer and a path to give her the fix today. Low: a support person asking the agent a question is close to a chatbot, and Front Row does the same flag move with more story.

C34.note: High: one mangled name shows the harm in five seconds, and the agent hunts edge cases with probes that code runs on a real copy. Low: migration safety tools exist (February's checker, June's migration winners) and Google Cloud is thin unless it rehearses on a Cloud SQL clone.

C35.note: High: captures why at the moment of change and acts when the reason expires. Low: the payoff needs a staged 'one year later', it borders LORE, and Google Cloud has no role.

C36.note: High: Kwame, and a failing test that turns a silent revert into an invitation back. Low: a narrower audience than operations, a second account and a staged revert, and little Google Cloud.

C37.note: High: a planted canary person proves end to end that deletion still deletes across real Google Cloud stores, for a person whose safety depends on it. Low: several real stores must exist and be searchable with keyless access, and the reveal needs a sentence of setup.

C38.note: High: the human go at every cue is the craft, rehearsed cue to cue on staging first, a natural Assisted prize story. Low: many moving parts keep show state across separate flow runs, and it could look like a fancy release checklist.

C39.note: High: turns the theme around, one person's lock stops every deploy, schedule and agent while she works, with a try-out that proves it. Low: freezes, schedule pauses and trigger toggles may need Maintainer, and Google Cloud appears only if Cloud Scheduler jobs get locked too.

C40.note: High: answers the theme with 'as far as everything can be undone' and hands a person exactly the one-way step. Low: on video it looks like another release gatekeeper and the person is barely there.

C41.note: High: finds finished fixes that never reached the customer and makes delivery one click for one named person. Low: close to stale MR nudge bots, and the daily pass list can read as a dashboard.

C42.note: High: the receiver speaks first and ownership moves only on a correct readback. Low: next to the banned handoff notes generator, needs two people on screen, and is mostly text comparison.

C43.note: High: an agent that actually runs runbook steps against staging Google Cloud resources and fixes the rot it finds. Low: the scene is a log, a restore drill needs real backups, and prose to commands can wander.

C44.note: High: the customer marks the exact records and code refuses anything else, so human confirmation is the safety feature. Low: a narrow operations task that needs a believable support round trip with one builder.

C45.note: High: natural Google Cloud depth (Cloud Run settings, Secret Manager names, keyless auth) and a model that never sees a secret. Low: the hero is a table with one red line, and it can look like a pre-deploy gate.

C46.note: High: Gloria's first phone-free holiday. Low: the output is a cast list and a script, people do all the work, and it needs months of seeded history.

C47.note: High: protects the responder and replies personally to everyone who wrote in. Low: answering stakeholder questions during an incident is a chatbot in disguise, which the brief excludes.

C48.note: High: real deploy cycles bring good work back one change at a time and find the bad one by elimination. Low: needs several fast pipelines with one truly bad change, and naming the culprit edges toward crowded root cause tools.

C49.note: High: looks along time instead of code structure and tries the future moment now on staging. Low: finding scheduled and date-driven code in general is hard to make convincing, and the demo is an issue list.

C50.note: High: starts from a marketer's calendar, load-tests Cloud Run staging for real and schedules temporary capacity, with a non-engineer as the hero. Low: honest load tests cost money and quota, and the wave must be a labelled simulation.

C51.note: High: an emergency lane that is fast but checked by code against a never-skip list, with the full run right after. Low: close to CrossCut's test selection (a June winner) and needs a slow demo pipeline.

C52.note: High: one command freezes every change in motion, other agents included, with a sensible resume order. Low: freezes may need Maintainer, and Lockout Tagout tells a stronger version with a person.

C53.note: High: treats a green after retry as evidence and proves a real race with a reproduction rate. Low: next to the excluded CI failure fixers, few stages, and no Google Cloud.

C54.note: High: covers the hours after a leak (contain on a person's go, check Cloud Audit Logs for misuse, stand down) and treats the new hire without blame. Low: detection sits in the crowded secrets space, and real rotation needs credentials a flow cannot read.

C55.note: High: a literal 'set intent and walk away' to production on the developer's own terms, where unclear means wait and ask. Low: few stages, numeric checks that resemble a gatekeeper, and a schedule start that may not count as human.

C56.note: High: credible hands-off merges for top-rated patches with code-set cooldowns and a staged supply chain catch. Low: supply chain scoring tools exist, it sits near crowded security bots, and nobody a viewer remembers.

C57.note: High: asks who was hurt instead of why it broke, computes credits in code, repairs failed orders after a dry run, and customers hear first. Low: needs accounts, plans and incident data that look real and are labelled demo.

top10.why: Priya's phone stays dark at 03:12 while the flag goes off under orders she signed at 22:00: approval as the feature, real Cloud Run action, lands in seconds.
Black screen, 'button, button, button': an agent with only a screen reader's view holds a release for Maria; the best 30-second moment in the pool.
A planted canary person proves deletion still deletes across Google Cloud stores after each release, for Laila, whose safety depends on it.
Clara's 2am Cloud Run fix is read from live config and Cloud Audit Logs, written back in her name, and the next deploy refuses to erase it.
Autonomy earned per action through a merge and revoked on the first miss; the most direct answer to how far agents may go without you.
A risky rollout run as numbered cues where only a person says go, rehearsed cue to cue on staging; the strongest Assisted prize story.
Mr. Haddad gets the fix first through a flag user list, and his 'works!' is what a person reads before widening it to everyone.
After an incident it works out who was hurt, computes credits in code, repairs failed orders after a dry run, and customers hear first.
Green monitors, three emails, one page that says 'I reproduced it'; then it adds the missing monitor and answers the nurse who asked if it was just her.
One person's padlock stops every deploy, schedule and agent while she repairs production by hand: the theme turned around.

traps.why: Looks like a top pick but is Night Orders' weaker twin: it changes nothing, reads as alert triage on video, and needs the same unverified night start.
On video it is a release gatekeeper, the most crowded space and the judges' own reference loop, and the person barely appears.
Rollback rehearsal is BABYDOV's turf, and old code on the new schema plus checksums can eat the build window.
The model only picks signals while scheduled code moves the flag, so the genuine AI use check and Innovation are at risk; days of rollout must be time compressed.
An incident chatbot in disguise, which the brief excludes.
Reads production logs after a merge, the Proof of Fix mechanism; strong Google Cloud use cannot rescue a scene with no person.
A report in disguise that judges will file next to Proof of Fix and Stayed Shipped.
A question and answer bot over records, next to crowded evidence receipts, with nothing to film.
GitLab already ships a Review instructions learner and LORE won on memory; it also needs other agents to be corrected before it can show anything.
Needs weeks of seeded metric and paging history; the hero is a replay chart that can look staged and dashboard-like.
Needs many past incidents with metrics, all generated; small-sample statistics on invented data invite doubt.
Conditional: if the pitch leads with 'your bug is fixed' emails it lands in the Proof of Fix family, and Service Desk email may need Maintainer; lead with the reporters-first rollout.
Sits beside the excluded CI failure fixers and needs weeks of staged retries by several people.
The hero moment is something not happening, and the model's share is thin.
